text: Real quantum noise is messy, asymmetric, and different on every piece of hardware. When researchers need one simple, honest, worst-case model to estimate whether an error-correcting code can actually work, they reach for the depolarizing channel.

Lesson 2 established that any single-qubit error reduces to the identity, X, Y, or Z. The depolarizing channel assigns a single total error probability, p, to a qubit, then splits that probability evenly across the three non-trivial error types: the probability of no error at all is 1 minus p, and the probability of X, Y, or Z individually is p over 3 each. So with probability 1 minus p nothing happens, and with the remaining probability p, one of the three Pauli errors occurs, each equally likely.

Here's exactly how that split works out. At p equals 0.001, there's a 99.9% chance of no error, and each of X, Y, and Z individually has about a 0.0333% chance. At p equals 0.01, that's 99% no error against roughly 0.333% each. And at p equals 0.05, 95% no error against roughly 1.667% each. Notice the pattern: whatever the total budget p is, exactly a third of it goes to each error type — no error type is ever favored over another.

This model has a special property: it looks exactly the same no matter which basis you use to describe the qubit — rewrite it in the plus-minus basis instead of zero-one, and you get the identical structure. That basis-independence is why it's the model of choice for threshold estimates, the calculations that answer whether physical error rates below some critical value make adding more qubits to a code actually help. Because the model doesn't secretly favor one error type, a threshold computed against it isn't accidentally tuned to flatter one particular correction strategy.

But be precise about its limits. Real superconducting and trapped-ion qubits typically show biased noise — dephasing, the Z-like errors tied to T2, is often more frequent than relaxation-driven bit-flips tied to T1, simply because T2 is often shorter than T1 in practice. Some advanced research deliberately exploits that asymmetry with biased-noise codes rather than assuming the symmetric picture. For this course, treat the depolarizing channel as the standard simplified yardstick quoted in threshold numbers and papers — useful and widely used, but explicitly not the full physical picture.
Next lesson separates two error sources that scale completely differently: gate errors, which pile up per operation, and decoherence errors, which pile up with elapsed time.
